caustica.options.rt.exposureMode.tooltip: How the ray-traced image is mapped to display brightness. Auto adapts to scene luminance; Manual uses the exposure value directly.
caustica.options.rt.manualEv.tooltip: Exposure compensation in stops. In Manual, this is the fixed exposure. In Auto, this biases the auto exposure brighter or darker.
caustica.options.rt.gamma.tooltip: Post-transform luminance gamma. Values below 1.00 brighten shadows and midtones while preserving black, white, and color ratios.
caustica.options.rt.spp.tooltip: Path-tracing samples taken per pixel each frame. Higher is cleaner but more demanding.
caustica.options.rt.maxBounces.tooltip: Maximum number of secondary path-tracing bounces after the primary hit. Higher captures more indirect light but costs more.
caustica.options.rt.entities.tooltip: Include entities and block entities in the ray-traced scene.
caustica.options.rt.particles.tooltip: Draw particles as camera-ray billboards inside the traced scene.
caustica.options.rt.glow.tooltip: Draw the vanilla Glowing-effect outline (through walls) around glowing entities.
caustica.options.rt.waterWaves.tooltip: Animate water-surface normals for moving wave highlights.
caustica.options.rt.volumetricFog.toolti: Haze and light shafts from an altitude-falling atmosphere, integrated along each traced ray so reflections and shadows get it too. The look dials are just below; the rest are in the config under rt.fog.*.
caustica.options.rt.fogDensity.tooltip:
Per-block extinction of the medium. Bedrock's own temperate biomes use 0.002 and its jungles a third more; at 0.01 the air is soup and at 0.05 you are painting with fog. Density at altitude falls off from this by the config's scale height.

Debug View 10 shows only what the medium itself contributed, so the haze you add here and the light it has to work with become separable.
caustica.options.rt.fogScaleHeight.toolt: How many blocks it takes for the medium to thin to a third of its density with altitude. Small values hug the ground and clear the sky; large ones make the whole world one uniform haze.
caustica.options.rt.fogAnisotropy.toolti: How much the medium throws light forward instead of everywhere. Low values make fog a uniform veil, high values carve beams out of it - and they also widen the glow around the sun, which the sky is already drawing, so past about 0.8 the haze starts erasing the very canopy the shafts come through. 0.6 is what Bedrock authors for temperate air; this is 0.8 because our fog is added on top of an atmosphere that already forward-scatters.
caustica.options.rt.fogSoftness.tooltip: How wide the sun is allowed to be when the light volume asks what is shadowed. The real disc is a quarter of a degree, so every ray agrees on it and a shaft's edge is either lit or not with nothing in between; a few degrees gives it a penumbra that widens with distance, which is what makes beams read as beams rather than as bright puffs. Judge it on the far canopy, not on the sun.
caustica.options.rt.fogSkyRays.tooltip: How finely each voxel integrates the sky it can see. This is the ambient veil rather than the shafts, so halving it is the cheapest thing to try when the F3 froxel lines are the complaint.
caustica.options.rt.fogSteps.tooltip: How finely each ray's path through the medium is resolved. The steps are placed where the light changes fastest, so raising this buys near-field detail -- beams ending, shade starting -- and never changes how far fog reaches. Cost is per ray bounce, so it is the second most expensive dial after samples.
caustica.options.rt.fogSunRays.tooltip: Shadow rays each voxel of the light volume throws at the sun. This is the resolution of a shaft's lighting rather than of its edges: with few rays a voxel answers whether the sun is out in ones and zeros, and the volume's temporal averaging is what turns that into a gradient. 0 removes direct sunlight from the fog entirely, leaving only skylight -- useful for seeing what the shafts actually are. Watch frame.traceFroxels in F3.
caustica.options.rt.fogHistory.tooltip: How many frames each voxel of the light volume averages. 1 is off: every voxel reports only this frame's rays, which reads as puffs between leaves because a few rays cannot answer a soft question. Long is smoother and lags when the camera moves fast; the volume fades its own history when the camera outruns a voxel, so this is a quality control and not a jitter control.
caustica.options.rt.fogFilter.tooltip: Smoothing across the voxels beside each other in a slice, applied to the sky term in full. It does not reach along the view ray or into the sun's transmittance, because that IS the shaft: see Fog Shaft Filter. Above 1.0 the kernel widens rather than the blend strengthening, which is how Minecraft RTX sizes its own volume blur against its history length.
caustica.options.rt.fogFilterSun.tooltip: How much of the voxel smoothing reaches into the sun's own transmittance instead of only the sky term. 0 leaves a shaft exactly as sharp as the light volume can carry it, which is what Minecraft RTX does. Raise it when the lattice between voxels bothers you more than soft edges do.
caustica.options.rt.fogRain.tooltip: How much a full downpour deepens the medium, ramped by the world's rain level. The participating-medium version of what vanilla does by swapping to its weather fog entry.
caustica.options.rt.fogGridDivisor.toolt: Screen pixels per edge of a light-volume voxel, so this is the resolution of every shaft edge. Halving it quadruples the voxels and the gather's rays -- frame.traceFroxels in F3 is that cost, measured. Changing it rebuilds the volume, which stalls a frame.
caustica.options.rt.hdr.tooltip: Recreate the swapchain for HDR (ST.2084/PQ) or native SDR output. Applied at the next frame boundary.
caustica.options.rt.hdrUiBrightness.tool: Absolute brightness (in nits) assigned to SDR-authored UI on an HDR display.
caustica.options.rt.hdrPeak.tooltip: Absolute brightness (in nits) highlights roll off toward. Set to your display's peak HDR brightness.
caustica.options.rt.dlssQuality.tooltip: DLSS Ray Reconstruction quality mode. Lower-quality modes render fewer pixels and upscale more aggressively for higher framerates; higher-quality modes render more pixels for a sharper image. Only affects the image when DLSS Ray Reconstruction is enabled.
caustica.options.rt.debugView.tooltip: Inspect ray-tracing buffers and exposure diagnostics after the normal frame has rendered.
